title: Vance blames Iran war for midterm rout; Trump says he 'would have done nothing different'
dek: Speaker Mike Johnson gives up the House Republican leadership and Iran's chief negotiator says Americans voted 'no to war'. What the split in Washington means for talks, the Strait of Hormuz and India.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Iran war has become the main fault line in Washington after the US midterm elections. Vice President JD Vance said on Wednesday that "the reason we lost is the war", House Speaker Mike Johnson said he would give up the leadership of House Republicans, and President Donald Trump said he would have done "nothing different". In Tehran, parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Americans had voted "NO TO WAR".

The split matters well beyond US politics. Talks to end the war, mediated by Qatar, have been stalled for months, the Strait of Hormuz remains largely shut to normal traffic, and Trump has said the US and Israel could return to full-scale war if no deal is reached. For India, which buys most of its oil from the Gulf and has lost seafarers in attacks on shipping, any decision in Washington on whether to escalate or settle directly affects fuel prices and the safety of Indian crews.

## What happened

In a long social media post on Wednesday, Vance blamed the conflict for the Republican defeat, in which Democrats won both houses of Congress. "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so," he wrote, according to one report. He listed the war, the cost of living, a sense that America was not being put first, and the US relationship with Israel as reasons Republican voters had backed Democrats. Another report said that he wrote: "the reason we lost is the war."

One report noted that Vance has said he will decide after the election whether to run for president in 2028, and that he had been noticeably quiet about the war after Trump launched it.

Trump, speaking to reporters at the White House the same day, accepted that the war had played a part but said it was worth fighting. "The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it," he said, according to one report. He said the war was needed to stop Tehran "having a nuclear weapon" and that he was fine with Vance's post. "I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different," he said.

In an earlier television interview, Trump said "a part of it was Iran", adding that voters agreed with his Iran policy but "probably weren't willing to do the short term consequences of paying more for gasoline", one report said. He said in another interview that the conflict would end "when I say it ends".

## Republicans regroup

Johnson told House Republicans in a letter, first reported by one outlet, that he would not seek a leadership post in the new Congress, in which his party will be in the minority. He pointed to the toll his three years as Speaker had taken on his family, one report said. "Serving as your Speaker has been the greatest professional honor of my life," he wrote.

Two Republicans have already launched bids to replace him as party leader in the House: Majority Leader Steve Scalise, who called the result "far worse than any of us expected", and Judiciary Committee chairman Jim Jordan, who called it "staggering". House Republicans are due to choose their leaders next week. Trump said he would "stay out of it", called Johnson "fantastic" and said he had not asked him to step aside, according to one report.

By early Wednesday afternoon in Washington, Democrats had taken at least 31 House seats from Republicans, according to one media count; some races were still being counted.

## What voters said

A news agency's survey of more than 100,000 voters found that about six in 10 thought the US had made the "wrong decision" in taking military action against Iran. But the war was not the top issue for most: about a third said it was "crucial" to their vote, compared with roughly half who said that about the cost of living or government corruption.

## Tehran's response

Ghalibaf, who is also Iran's chief negotiator in the indirect talks, wrote on X that Iran "endorsed" the American voters' message. "If the US [government] betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," he warned, according to one report.

President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Tuesday that his government was trying to resolve the crisis "through dialogue" and that "no-one will benefit from this war" if it resumed. Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said on Monday that the talks were still based on a seven-step proposal Iran submitted in September, which had been "condensed" so it could be carried out within two days.

The Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, took a harder line in a statement on Wednesday, saying anyone who expected a change in American "hostility" was mistaken and that a renewed war would have "much wider dimensions".

## At sea

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday that four oil tankers had caught fire after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz and that two more had been intercepted. One broadcaster's verification unit said it had found no evidence that four tankers were destroyed. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO) said one tanker was hit by two unknown projectiles about 14 nautical miles north-east of Limah, on Oman's Musandam peninsula, on Tuesday evening, and that no one was hurt. None of the IRGC's claims has been independently confirmed.

On Monday, an Indian crew member of a dhow was killed in an attack north-east of Limah; 13 other crew were rescued by Omani authorities.

## Background

The US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February. A preliminary deal reached in June to end the fighting and reopen the Strait collapsed within weeks, after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reimposed its naval blockade, according to one report. About a fifth of the world's oil and gas normally passes through the Strait. In an interview before the vote, Trump said the US was "locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no need for it".

## What it means for India

The new Congress takes office in January. With majorities in both houses, Democrats will be able to hold votes on war funding and war powers and to open investigations, though Trump keeps his veto and remains commander-in-chief. Until then, Republicans control both houses, which leaves two months in which the administration can still choose to escalate or to settle.

For India, either path matters. A return to all-out war would put more Indian ships and seafarers at risk and push oil prices higher; a settlement that reopens the Strait would ease import costs. An Iranian MP said this week that Indian ships are exempt from Iran's transit curbs but still pay fees; New Delhi has not commented on that claim.

## What happens next

- House Republicans choose new leaders next week.
- Qatar, the mediator, has not said when the next round of indirect talks will take place.
- The new Congress is sworn in on 3 January 2027.
